Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This article belongs to a series on geometric complexity theory (GCT), an approach to the P vs. NP and related problems through algebraic geometry and representation theory. The basic principle behind this approach is called the flip. In essence, it reduces the negative hypothesis in complexity theory (the lower bound problems), such as the P vs. NP problem in characteristic zero, to the positive hypothesis in complexity theory (the upper bound problems): specifically, to showing that the problems of deciding nonvanishing of the fundamental structural constants in representation theory and algebraic geometry, such as the well known plethysm constants--or rather certain relaxed forms of these decision probelms--belong to the complexity class P. In this article, we suggest a plan for implementing the flip, i.e., for showing that these relaxed decision problems belong to P. This is based on the reduction of the preceding complexity-theoretic positive hypotheses to mathematical positivity hypotheses: specifically, to showing that there exist positive formulae--i.e. formulae with nonnegative coefficients--for the structural constants under consideration and certain functions associated with them. These turn out be intimately related to the similar positivity properties of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials and the multiplicative structural constants of the canonical (global crystal) bases in the theory of Drinfeld-Jimbo quantum groups. The known proofs of these positivity properties depend on the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and the related results. Thus the reduction here, in conjunction with the flip, in essence, says that the validity of the P vs. NP conjecture in characteristic zero is intimately linked to the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and related problems.

outputs.L1:
This article is part of a series on geometric complexity theory (GCT), an approach to the P vs. NP problem and related questions through algebraic geometry and representation theory. The basic principle underlying this approach is known as the flip. In essence, the flip reduces negative hypotheses in complexity theory—namely, lower-bound problems such as P vs. NP in characteristic zero—to positive hypotheses concerning upper-bound problems. More specifically, it reduces them to showing that certain relaxed forms of the decision problems for the nonvanishing of fundamental structural constants in representation theory and algebraic geometry—such as the well-known plethysm constants—belong to the complexity class P.

In this article, we propose a plan for implementing the flip; that is, for proving that these relaxed decision problems belong to P. The plan is based on reducing the preceding complexity-theoretic positive hypotheses to mathematical positivity hypotheses—specifically, to establishing the existence of positive formulae, meaning formulae with nonnegative coefficients, for the structural constants under consideration and for certain functions associated with them.

These positivity hypotheses turn out to be intimately related to analogous positivity properties of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials and of the multiplicative structural constants of canonical (global crystal) bases in the theory of Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum groups. The known proofs of these positivity properties depend on the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and related results. Thus, in conjunction with the flip, the reduction presented here says, in essence, that the validity of the P vs. NP conjecture in characteristic zero is intimately linked to the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and related problems.

This paper is part of a broader collection devoted to geometric complexity theory (GCT), which uses algebraic geometry and representation theory to investigate P versus NP and related questions. At the heart of GCT lies a strategy known as the “flip.” Roughly speaking, the flip transforms negative complexity-theoretic assertions—lower-bound questions such as P versus NP over fields of characteristic zero—into positive, upper-bound assertions. More precisely, it seeks to prove that certain relaxed versions of the decision problems for determining whether fundamental structural constants in representation theory and algebraic geometry are nonzero—including the classical plethysm constants—lie in the complexity class P.

The present article proposes a program for carrying out this strategy and establishing polynomial-time algorithms for those relaxed decision problems. Its central step is to replace the relevant positive hypotheses from complexity theory with mathematical positivity conjectures. In particular, the goal is to establish positive formulas, meaning expressions whose coefficients are all nonnegative, for the structural constants in question and for certain associated functions.

These conjectured positivity phenomena are closely connected to analogous positivity results for Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials and for the multiplicative structural constants of canonical, or global crystal, bases in the theory of Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum groups. Existing proofs of those analogous results rely on the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and related theorems. Consequently, when this reduction is combined with the flip, it suggests that the P versus NP conjecture in characteristic zero is deeply connected to the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields and associated questions.

Geometric complexity theory (GCT) is a program for studying the P versus NP problem and related complexity-class separations through tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory. Rather than attacking computational lower bounds directly, GCT translates them into questions about algebraic varieties, group actions, representations, and associated structural constants.

A central principle of the program, known as the **flip**, seeks to transform difficult lower-bound problems into constructive upper-bound problems. More specifically, it reduces the task of proving complexity lower bounds to showing that certain relaxed nonvanishing decision problems for representation-theoretic structural constants can be solved in polynomial time. In this way, the flip aims to replace an intractable search for obstructions with an efficient procedure for recognizing them.

The article proposes implementing this strategy by reducing the required complexity-theoretic upper bounds to mathematical **positivity hypotheses**. These hypotheses assert the existence of suitable formulas or combinatorial descriptions in which all coefficients are nonnegative. Such positive formulas can make nonvanishing easier to decide, potentially yielding the polynomial-time algorithms required by the flip.

The proposed hypotheses are closely connected to established positivity phenomena in representation theory, particularly the positivity of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials and of structural constants associated with canonical bases in quantum group theory. These classical results provide important models for the kinds of positivity statements that GCT seeks in more general settings.

Significantly, known proofs of several of these representation-theoretic positivity results depend on deep geometric methods ultimately linked to the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields. GCT therefore suggests a striking conceptual connection: resolving major complexity-theoretic questions such as P versus NP in characteristic zero may require positivity theorems whose foundations are related to the finite-field Riemann hypothesis. This does not by itself establish a formal equivalence, but it indicates that the mathematical structures underlying computational complexity may be intertwined with some of the deepest results in arithmetic geometry.

Geometric complexity theory (GCT) is a program for attacking the P versus NP problem by translating computational lower bounds into questions in algebraic geometry and representation theory. Working over a field of characteristic zero, it studies algebraic analogues of complexity classes, most notably the separation of the permanent from the determinant. The determinant can be computed efficiently and has rich symmetry, whereas the permanent encodes problems believed to be intractable. After embedding these polynomials into suitable representation spaces, GCT seeks to prove that the permanent cannot be obtained from a determinant of polynomially bounded size, even after taking limits. Geometrically, this becomes a problem of separating orbit closures under the action of a general linear group.

A central feature of GCT is the “flip.” Instead of proving a lower bound directly by analyzing every possible efficient algorithm, the flip aims to produce explicit certificates—called obstructions—that demonstrate the required separation. These obstructions are usually labels of irreducible representations whose multiplicities behave differently in the coordinate rings of the relevant orbit closures. For the approach to yield a feasible proof rather than merely an abstract existence argument, such obstructions should be constructible and verifiable in polynomial time.

This requirement leads to difficult decision problems involving representation-theoretic and algebraic-geometric structural constants. Examples include variants of Littlewood–Richardson, Kronecker, and plethysm multiplicities, as well as multiplicities associated with coordinate rings and orbit closures. One would like efficient procedures for deciding whether these quantities are nonzero. In many cases GCT first considers a relaxed or asymptotic version of nonvanishing: instead of asking whether a multiplicity attached to a given set of parameters is positive, one asks whether it becomes positive after the parameters are scaled, or whether the corresponding point lies in an associated moment or multiplicity cone.

The hoped-for route to polynomial-time algorithms is through positivity. A positive formula expresses a structural constant as a sum or count of explicitly defined nonnegative contributions, with no cancellation. Such a formula can turn nonvanishing into the existence of a feasible combinatorial or geometric object. If the relevant feasible region has suitable polyhedral descriptions and saturation properties, relaxed nonvanishing can often be decided by linear programming or related polynomial-time methods. Thus the GCT program introduces positivity and saturation hypotheses intended to show that these decision problems lie in P.

This is not simply a demand for elegant combinatorial formulas. General algebraic formulas may contain positive and negative terms whose cancellations are extremely difficult to control. By contrast, a formula with nonnegative coefficients makes nonvanishing structurally transparent. The flip therefore replaces the original lower-bound problem with a collection of explicit mathematical tasks: construct appropriate obstruction families, establish positive formulas for the multiplicities governing them, prove the necessary saturation or asymptotic properties, and design efficient algorithms based on those results.

The depth of these positivity requirements becomes clearer from precedents in representation theory. Fundamental positivity theorems for Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, intersection cohomology, and canonical bases were not obtained by elementary manipulation alone. Their proofs use geometric constructions over finite fields, purity of Frobenius eigenvalues, and results belonging to the circle of ideas surrounding the Weil conjectures and the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields. In these settings, coefficients that initially arise from alternating or cancellation-prone expressions are shown to be nonnegative because they can be interpreted through graded geometric or cohomological objects with strong purity properties.

GCT suggests that the positivity phenomena needed for complexity theory may require comparably deep mathematics. The analogy does not mean that resolving P versus NP is a direct consequence of the classical Riemann hypothesis, nor that existing finite-field theorems already prove the required GCT conjectures. Rather, it indicates that the structural constants arising in complexity may possess hidden geometric explanations, and that proving their positivity could demand new analogues of the machinery that established positivity for Kazhdan–Lusztig theory and canonical bases.

From this perspective, the P versus NP problem is connected to arithmetic geometry in a precise methodological sense. The search for efficient obstruction certificates leads to representation-theoretic nonvanishing problems; efficient nonvanishing tests lead to positive formulas and saturation statements; and precedents for such positivity point toward geometry over finite fields, purity, and Riemann-hypothesis-type results. The GCT program thus presents lower bounds not as isolated combinatorial impossibility statements, but as consequences of a broader theory of symmetry, geometry, and positivity. Its ambitious claim is that progress on computational complexity may depend on uncovering structural phenomena as deep as those that have transformed modern algebraic geometry and representation theory.

counterfactuals.output: Geometric complexity theory (GCT) recasts the characteristic-zero \(P\) versus \(NP\) problem as separating orbit closures associated with the determinant and permanent. Its “flip” replaces the task of proving lower bounds against all efficient algorithms with the constructive search for explicit representation-theoretic obstructions—irreducible modules occurring on one orbit closure but not the other. Positivity and saturation hypotheses for the relevant multiplicities are intended to make these obstructions efficiently decidable and constructible. GCT further proposes that such positivity should follow from geometric models over finite fields: multiplicities would be encoded by point counts or cohomological data, whose regularity and nonnegativity are controlled by the Weil conjectures, especially the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields. Thus the flip outlines a conditional bridge from complexity lower bounds to positivity in representation theory and, ultimately, to arithmetic geometry.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the proposed GCT strategy for reducing complexity lower bounds to polynomial-time nonvanishing problems for plethysm constants and related structural constants.
counterfactuals.output:
The GCT program reframes an arithmetic lower bound—most notably \(\mathrm{perm}\notin \mathrm{VP}\), or equivalently the permanent not being a polynomial-size projection/degeneration of the determinant—as an orbit-closure separation problem under a linear group action.

Its proposed reduction works as follows:

1. **Associate varieties to complexity classes.**  
   The “easy” model, such as the determinant, defines a class variety \(X_{\mathrm{det}}\); the hard polynomial, such as the permanent, defines \(X_{\mathrm{perm}}\). A lower bound follows if
   \[
   X_{\mathrm{perm}}\not\subseteq X_{\mathrm{det}}.
   \]

2. **Decompose coordinate rings into representations.**  
   The graded coordinate rings of these varieties are decomposed into irreducible \(GL\)-modules. Their multiplicities are governed by plethysm coefficients and related structural constants, including Kronecker-type coefficients and constants attached to proposed “nonstandard” quantum groups.

3. **Use an occurrence or multiplicity obstruction.**  
   A partition/highest weight \(\lambda\) is an obstruction if the corresponding representation occurs on the hard side but not, or with insufficient multiplicity, on the easy side. Such a discrepancy certifies noncontainment and hence the desired lower bound.

4. **Reduce verification to nonvanishing.**  
   Checking an obstruction becomes a collection of questions of the form
   \[
   a_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}>0?
   \]
   for the relevant plethysm or structural constants. The labels are intended to have polynomial bit length, so a proposed obstruction can be verified efficiently if these positivity questions are in polynomial time.

5. **Obtain polynomial time through positivity and saturation.**  
   GCT conjectures that these constants admit positive combinatorial/polyhedral formulas: a constant is the number of lattice points in an explicitly described polytope. A suitable saturation theorem would then make nonvanishing equivalent, up to controlled exceptional cases, to nonemptiness of the rational polytope. Rational feasibility can be decided in polynomial time by linear-programming or ellipsoid methods, without computing the often enormous coefficient itself.

Thus the “flip” in GCT is to replace the direct construction of hard functions by the construction of short, efficiently checkable representation-theoretic obstructions. The overall program is conditional: the required positivity, saturation, and efficient-description properties for general plethysm and nonstandard structural constants remain major unresolved parts of the strategy, and simple occurrence obstructions are known to face limitations in some formulations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic introduction to a paper in the geometric complexity theory series, focusing on positive formulae, canonical bases, Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, and their relevance to P vs. NP.
counterfactuals.output:
## Introduction

The problem of separating \(\mathsf{P}\) from \(\mathsf{NP}\) is usually formulated in terms of algorithms, reductions, and resource bounds. Geometric complexity theory (GCT) seeks to recast this problem as one in algebraic geometry and representation theory. In its basic form, the program compares algebraic complexity classes through orbit closures associated with complete polynomials—most prominently the determinant and the permanent—under the action of a general linear group. A sufficiently strong separation between these orbit closures would imply lower bounds for arithmetic computation and, through the standard connections between arithmetic and Boolean complexity, would bear directly on the \(\mathsf{P}\) versus \(\mathsf{NP}\) problem. The central task is therefore to identify representation-theoretic invariants that distinguish the relevant varieties and that can be constructed and verified with complexity-theoretically feasible resources.

A natural class of proposed invariants consists of *obstructions*: irreducible representations whose multiplicities differ in the coordinate rings associated with the “easy” and “hard” sides of the comparison. In the determinant-versus-permanent setting, one studies graded coordinate rings of suitable orbit closures and asks whether a highest weight representation occurs on one side but not the other, or occurs with quantitatively different multiplicity. This reformulation is conceptually powerful, but it transfers the original difficulty into questions about plethysm coefficients, Kronecker coefficients, branching multiplicities, and related structural constants. These quantities are notoriously difficult to compute, and their definitions as alternating sums or dimensions of indirectly specified spaces often conceal the positivity and regularity needed for a useful obstruction theory.

The search for *positive formulae* is intended to address this difficulty. By a positive formula we mean, broadly, a combinatorial or geometric description of a multiplicity as the cardinality of an explicitly defined set, the number of lattice points in a polytope, or a sum of manifestly nonnegative contributions. Such a formula does more than certify that a coefficient is nonnegative. If sufficiently explicit and uniform, it can convert representation-theoretic occurrence into an algorithmic decision problem, support saturation or quasipolynomiality results, and make possible the efficient verification of candidate obstructions. Positivity is thus not merely an aesthetic property: within GCT it is expected to connect structural representation theory with the computational requirements of constructing and recognizing lower-bound certificates.

The paradigmatic source of this expectation is the theory of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. Introduced through the Hecke algebra of a Coxeter group, these polynomials initially arise from a basis defined by bar invariance and triangularity, rather than from a manifestly positive combinatorial rule. Their coefficients nevertheless admit deep geometric interpretations in terms of intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties. The resulting positivity theorem transformed Kazhdan–Lusztig theory into a central tool in representation theory, with applications to character formulae, category \(\mathcal O\), singularities of Schubert varieties, and the structure of Hecke-algebra modules. This history suggests a general strategy: when a representation-theoretic multiplicity appears opaque or alternating, one should search for a hidden geometric or categorical model in which it becomes the dimension of a naturally graded space.

Canonical and global crystal bases provide a closely related model. In quantum groups and their representations, these bases impose integral, positivity, and compatibility properties that are invisible in arbitrary coordinates. Their structure constants frequently lie in semirings such as \(\mathbb{N}[q,q^{-1}]\), while specialization and crystal limits yield combinatorial parametrizations of basis elements and tensor-product components. Canonical bases therefore offer a possible bridge between geometry, representation theory, and algorithms: they may turn multiplicity spaces into objects indexed by discrete data, and they may reveal the polyhedral or categorical structures underlying positive formulae. From the GCT perspective, the relevant question is whether analogous bases can be constructed for the nonstandard representation-theoretic objects arising from plethysm, orbit closures, and the comparison of determinant- and permanent-type varieties.

This paper develops that question as part of the broader GCT program. Our guiding principle is that the required positivity phenomena should not be imposed externally on multiplicity functions, but should arise from an appropriate analogue of the canonical-basis/Kazhdan–Lusztig framework. We investigate algebras and modules naturally associated with the relevant symmetry groups and formulate conditions under which distinguished bases would yield positive expressions for their structural constants and multiplicities. Particular emphasis is placed on three logically separate issues: the existence of a canonical or geometrically defined basis; positivity of the corresponding transition and structure coefficients; and the algorithmic accessibility of the combinatorial data indexing that basis. The last condition is essential: a positive formula of exponential descriptive complexity would have limited value for complexity-theoretic applications.

The role of Kazhdan–Lusztig theory in this investigation is both technical and methodological. Technically, its geometric realizations provide templates involving stratifications, perverse sheaves, intersection cohomology, and purity, each of which can force positivity. Methodologically, it demonstrates that positivity may become visible only after replacing a classical algebra by a deformation and replacing naive coordinates by a basis adapted to duality and geometry. We accordingly examine whether the multiplicity problems arising in GCT admit suitable deformations, categorical lifts, or moduli-theoretic interpretations. A successful construction would ideally specialize to the classical representation-theoretic quantities while retaining enough graded structure to produce polynomial refinements analogous to Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials.

Several qualifications are important. First, positivity alone does not imply a separation of complexity classes. Even when multiplicities have positive descriptions, occurrence obstructions may fail to exist in a proposed form, or may not be sufficiently abundant or explicit. Indeed, results on orbit closures and representation-theoretic multiplicities have exposed substantial limitations of the simplest obstruction strategies. Second, canonical bases are not automatically algorithmic: their definition may depend on geometric or categorical machinery whose effective complexity remains uncontrolled. Third, the passage from algebraic lower bounds to \(\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}\) involves additional uniformity and modeling issues. The purpose of the present approach is therefore not to claim a resolution of \(\mathsf{P}\) versus \(\mathsf{NP}\), but to isolate and study structural positivity hypotheses that could make representation-theoretic obstruction methods mathematically and computationally viable.

Viewed in this way, positive formulae, canonical bases, and Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials form three aspects of a common research agenda. Positive formulae supply verifiable descriptions of multiplicities; canonical bases organize those descriptions in a representation-theoretically natural manner; and Kazhdan–Lusztig theory provides the leading example of how hidden geometry can produce both positivity and computable structure. Their relevance to complexity theory lies in the possibility that lower-bound certificates can be translated into explicit, finite, and efficiently checkable representation-theoretic data. Establishing such a translation remains a major open challenge, but it offers a precise setting in which advances in geometric representation theory may contribute to the foundational questions of computational complexity.

counterfactuals.output: In geometric complexity theory (GCT), the “flip” recasts hard circuit lower bounds—such as separating permanent from determinant orbit closures—as the constructive problem of exhibiting efficiently verifiable representation-theoretic obstructions; making this strategy algorithmic depends on positivity and saturation-type properties for multiplicities and related structural constants. For classical representation theory, analogous positivity is explained by canonical or crystal bases associated with Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum groups: relevant tensor-product and coordinate-ring structure constants become Laurent polynomials with nonnegative coefficients, often through geometric realizations by perverse sheaves or intersection cohomology. These geometric constructions are defined over finite fields, where purity and the required sign/positivity behavior are controlled by Deligne’s Riemann hypothesis over finite fields—the weight theorem underlying the Weil conjectures. GCT therefore proposes that suitable “nonstandard” quantum groups and canonical bases attached to complexity-theoretic orbit problems should yield the positivity needed for the flip, with a prospective proof modeled on the same chain linking quantum groups, geometric representation theory, and finite-field Riemann-hypothesis methods; this is a research program and analogy, not an established derivation of complexity lower bounds from the Riemann hypothesis.

counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** Geometric complexity theory (GCT) seeks explicit representation-theoretic obstructions separating complexity classes, while its proposed “flip” replaces the direct construction of lower-bound witnesses by efficient algorithms for deciding their existence. We formulate a program for implementing this flip through polynomial-time algorithms for relaxed nonvanishing problems associated with multiplicity functions arising in the coordinate rings of orbit closures. The central proposal is to encode candidate obstructions by succinct highest-weight data and reduce their asymptotic nonvanishing to feasibility in explicitly described rational polyhedra or, more generally, to membership in saturated representation-theoretic semigroups. We isolate the structural ingredients needed for polynomial-time decidability: polynomially bounded certificates, efficient separation oracles, robust saturation or positivity theorems, and effective control of the gap between relaxed and exact multiplicities. We then outline a staged strategy combining moment-polytope methods, invariant theory, and convex optimization to obtain algorithms polynomial in the bit length of the input parameters. Particular attention is given to uniformity, boundary cases, and the lifting of relaxed nonvanishing certificates to genuine obstruction labels. The resulting framework identifies precise mathematical and algorithmic milestones whose resolution would convert the existence of GCT obstructions into an explicit, verifiable search procedure. Although the program is conditional on new positivity and saturation results, it provides a concrete route for realizing the GCT flip and clarifies how representation-theoretic structure could support efficient obstruction discovery.
